summary: Defines a way to query for reputation information using HTTP with JSON as the payload format. It is part of a small family of reputation documents.

plainLanguage.summary: A simple way to ask a website how trusted a name is.

questions: how to query reputation over http
what is a reputation query protocol
what happens if a reputation application is unknown
subtitle: How a client asks a reputation service about a name: fetch a URI template, fill it in, send a GET.

tldr.problem: Clients that want reputation data about an entity need a standard way to ask a reputation service without hard-coding the service's URL layout.
tldr.mechanism: The client fetches a URI template from the well-known location repute-template on the service host, fills in application, service, subject and optionally assertion, and issues an HTTP GET for the result.
tldr.outcome: The reply is expected to be an application/reputon+json document defined in RFC 7071. Service discovery and authentication are left out of scope.

facts.label: Default template lifetime
facts.value: One day, when no Expires field is present

today: RFC 7072 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the media type defined in RFC 7071.

sections.title: A Two-Stage Query
sections.content:
RFC 7072 defines a way to query a reputation data service about an entity. The transport is HTTP and the payload format is JSON. The query is made in two stages. First, the client retrieves a template from the server describing how to build a URI. Second, the client uses the constructed URI to request the reputation data.

A query has these components: the subject, the host name or IP address of the service, the name of the reputation application (the context in which the subject is evaluated) and, optionally, the names of specific assertions wanted.
sections.plainLanguage: You ask for a form, then you fill it in and send it back. The form tells you exactly how to write your question.

sections.title: What Is Not Covered
sections.content:
There is no discovery protocol for finding reputation services. They are typically subscription services, negotiated between operators out of band. Authentication between client and server is also outside the specification, although the RFC says it could come through transport-based or object-based mechanisms, or a later extension.

The application name is expected to be one registered in the "Reputation Applications" registry defined in RFC 7071. A server that gets a query for an application it does not recognize or explicitly support MUST return a 404 error code.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC does not tell you which services exist or how to log in. You have to arrange that with the service yourself.

sections.title: Fetching the Template
sections.content:
The client requests the well-known URI repute-template from the host providing the service, using HTTP. The reply MUST use the text/plain media type and SHOULD include an Expires field saying how long clients may keep the template.

If Expires is present, the client SHOULD NOT query the same server again before that time. If it is absent, the client SHOULD wait at least one day, which is the default expiration. The file may hold several templates, each separated by a carriage return (0x0D) and newline (0x0A). The client expands each template that uses a URI scheme it supports, in file order, until it finds one it can connect to.
sections.plainLanguage: The form can be kept for a while, so you do not have to ask for it each time. If nobody says how long, ask for a fresh one after a day.

sections.title: Template Variables
sections.content:
The template follows the URI Template format. Clients MUST supply three values:

  • application: the reputation application name, a MIME token.
  • service: the host name or IP address queried. It MUST be the same host the template was fetched from.
  • subject: the subject of the query, matching the MIME value syntax.

An assertion variable (a MIME token) may also be given. If absent, the client is asking for all available assertion information. For an optional variable with no value, the client substitutes the empty string, so providers MUST write templates that still yield a valid, unambiguous URI. The RFC warns that adjacent slashes from empty path components can be collapsed by servers, and recommends forms such as {?a,b}.

Applications can add required or optional query parameters when they register with IANA. Providers may add private ones, which are not registered.
sections.plainLanguage: The blanks you must fill in are the topic, the service, and who or what you are asking about. You may also say which exact question you want answered.

sections.title: The Response
sections.content:
The response is expected to use the application/reputon+json media type defined in RFC 7071. If the server sends an HTTP Expires field, that timestamp MUST align with the expires field inside the response, if any. Otherwise the response could expire while the HTTP reply has not, and the client could not obtain a fresh answer.

A client must implement HTTP to fetch the template, so a server can assume the client handles a template that produces an http URI. A template could yield another scheme, which the client may try if it supports it. A server SHOULD offer service over HTTP and publish templates saying so, as a baseline for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: The answer comes back as a report card, and its "use by" time must match the one on the envelope it came in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it defines particular uses of existing protocols and introduces no new security considerations of its own. It notes that fetching the template over basic HTTP is not secure without certain extensions. The HTTP security considerations apply, and HTTP over TLS can be used to conceal the query and its response.

The validity and use of reputation information is called an obvious security concern, but it is beyond the scope of this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking over plain HTTP is like shouting your question across a room. If you want privacy, use the encrypted version.
